sections.heading: Why we are writing to you

sentences.text: We are writing from the HNRNPU-related epileptic encephalopathy community to your SLC6A1-related epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures community because public records show both conditions are linked with too little protein from one lost copy, and the recorded mechanism for each condition is loss of function with definitive gene-disease support.

Public records also show a high phenotype similarity between the two conditions, with shared features that include atonic seizure, generalized non-motor absence seizure, non-motor seizure, dialeptic seizure, and myoclonus.
Gene2Phenotype records definitive gene links for both HNRNPU and SLC6A1.
Gene2Phenotype also records loss of function, inferred from variant types, for both conditions.
Public records show both communities have patient organizations, and both conditions are also included in broader research efforts such as Simons Searchlight.
Public records show both conditions also have disease models reported in the research literature.

sections.heading: What we would like to learn from or reuse

sentences.text: We would like to learn from your registry and natural history work, because public records show SLC6A1-related studies include the SLC6A1-NDD Prospective Longitudinal Natural History Study, Simons Searchlight, Citizen Health, and an SLC6A1 Connect registry.

Public records suggest that registry items, consent language, visit schedules, and outcome measures may be useful starting points for our community, but age of onset and severity still need expert review before anything is adopted.

We would also like to learn which clinics, sites, and investigators your community works with, because public records show routes through Simons Searchlight, Citizen Health, SLC6A1 Connect, and several SLC6A1 studies.

We would value any advice on trial design, because public records show SLC6A1 has targeted interventional studies in gene therapy and small molecules, and those designs may be useful templates for expert review in HNRNPU.
Public records show more formal study activity for SLC6A1 than for HNRNPU at this time.
We found no public record of active NIH-funded HNRNPU projects in fiscal years 2025 to 2026, while public records show two active NIH-funded SLC6A1 projects in that period.
We found no public record of a targeted HNRNPU clinical trial, while ClinicalTrials.gov records for SLC6A1 include two gene-level targeted trials with highest phase 2.

We also need to be careful about mechanism, because the recorded mechanism is made at the gene-and-disease level, not for every family, and a clinical geneticist should confirm whether a child's own HNRNPU variant is loss of function, gain of function, or dominant negative before people borrow treatment logic from another condition.
We also understand that the recorded loss-of-function mechanism for both conditions is inferred from variant types rather than shown by direct functional evidence.
Because of that, we must not assume that an SLC6A1 therapeutic strategy, assay, or trial design will apply directly to HNRNPU without expert review.
We also must not assume that a person with HNRNPU would be eligible for an SLC6A1 trial, because public records do not assert that, and the study teams would need to advise directly.
Public records also note that the SLC6A1 Connect organization listing was auto-checked and not yet human verified, so we would want to confirm the right contact and whether it runs a registry now.
Do the age of onset and typical severity in SLC6A1-related disease match HNRNPU closely enough for registry items and outcome measures to carry over well.
Is SLC6A1 Connect the right community contact, and does it run a registry at this time.
Has a child's specific HNRNPU variant been functionally classified, and does it match the mechanism recorded for the condition.
What direct functional evidence exists for HNRNPU, given that the recorded mechanism is inferred from variant types.
Thank you for reading.

glossary.meaning: A gene change that leads to too little working protein.
A study that follows people over time to learn how a condition changes.
A feature researchers track to see how a person is doing over time.
A doctor with specialist training in genetic conditions and variant interpretation.
The signs and symptoms a person has.
A lab cell or animal system used to study a condition.
